title: What is a transaction? Explain the ACID properties with the help of a bank transfer example.
chunks: A transaction is a logical unit of work consisting of one or more SQL statements that must be executed entirely or not at all. ACID Properties (Bank Transfer Example: A to B): Atomicity : "All or nothing." If money is deducted from A, it MUST be credited to B. If either fails, the entire transaction is rolled back. Consistency : The database must remain in a valid state. The total sum of A + B's balances must be the same before and after the transaction. Isolation : Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. If another transaction reads A's balance during the transfer, it will see the state either strictly before or strictly after, not midway. Durability : Once the transaction is committed, the changes are permanent and will survive system crashes. Transaction State Diagram
subject: dbms

title: Explain COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT with a suitable example on the ACCOUNT table.
chunks: COMMIT : Saves all changes made during the current transaction permanently. ROLLBACK : Undoes all changes made during the current transaction, reverting to the last commit. SAVEPOINT : Sets a marker within a transaction so you can roll back to that specific point without canceling the entire transaction. START TRANSACTION; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A101'; SAVEPOINT step1; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 500 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; -- If something goes wrong here: ROLLBACK TO step1; -- Undoes only the A102 update COMMIT; -- Saves the final state
subject: dbms

title: Write a transaction that transfers Rs. 3000 from account A102 to account A103, placing a SAVEPOINT just before the transfer, and finally commit it.
chunks: START TRANSACTION; SAVEPOINT before_transfer; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance - 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A102'; UPDATE ACCOUNT SET Balance = Balance + 3000 WHERE Acc_No = 'A103'; COMMIT;
subject: dbms

title: Using a searched CASE statement, classify each account's Balance as 'High' if it is 25000 or more, 'Medium' if it is 15000 or more, and 'Low' otherwise.
chunks: SELECT Acc_No, Name, Balance, CASE WHEN Balance >= 25000 THEN 'High' WHEN Balance >= 15000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Low' END AS Balance_Category FROM ACCOUNT;

title: In one or two lines each, state the purpose of a stored procedure, a sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT in MySQL), a cursor and a trigger.
chunks: Stored Procedure : A pre-compiled collection of SQL statements saved in the database that can be executed as a single callable routine. Sequence (AUTO_INCREMENT) : Automatically generates unique, sequential numeric values, typically used for primary keys. Cursor : A database object used to retrieve and process rows one by one from a result set inside a stored procedure. Trigger : A special type of stored procedure that automatically executes (fires) in response to specific DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a table.
subject: dbms

title: What is the difference between a BEFORE trigger and an AFTER trigger? What do the keywords NEW and OLD refer to inside a trigger?
chunks: BEFORE Trigger executes before the triggering DML operation is applied (useful for validation/modification of incoming data). AFTER Trigger executes after the operation (useful for auditing or cascading changes to other tables). NEW refers to the incoming data (being inserted or updated). OLD refers to the existing data in the table before the operation (being updated or deleted).
subject: dbms

title: What is the purpose of exception handling in a stored procedure? Briefly explain DECLARE ... HANDLER and the SIGNAL statement.
chunks: Exception handling ensures that if an error occurs during execution, the stored procedure can catch it and gracefully handle it (e.g., rolling back a transaction) instead of crashing. DECLARE ... HANDLER : Defines a block of code to execute when a specific error or condition occurs (e.g., DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION ). SIGNAL : Used to artificially raise a custom error or exception, returning a custom SQLSTATE and message to the caller.
subject: dbms

Unit I: Introduction to DBMS CO1

Architecture & Data Independence U1 The 3-schema architecture separates user views (External), logic (Conceptual), and storage (Internal). It ensures data independence, allowing changes in one schema without affecting others. Example: Changing file structure from sequential to B+ tree (Physical Independence) doesn't alter SQL queries at the Conceptual level. Pro-Tip: Logical data independence is much harder to achieve than physical, as application logic tightly binds to the conceptual schema.

Keys & Constraints U1 Super keys identify tuples uniquely. Candidate keys are minimal super keys. Primary keys are chosen candidate keys. Foreign keys enforce referential integrity between tables. Example: `{EmpID, Email}` is a Super Key. `EmpID` is a Candidate and Primary Key. Exam Trap: A relation can have multiple candidate keys but strictly ONE primary key. Nulls are not allowed in PKs (Entity Integrity).

Normalization: 1NF to BCNF U1 1NF mandates atomic domains. 2NF removes partial dependencies (non-prime depends on part of PK). 3NF eliminates transitive dependencies. BCNF strictly enforces every determinant as a candidate key. Example: If `City -> Zip` and `Zip -> State`, `City -> State` is a transitive dependency violating 3NF. Exam Trap: BCNF decomposition may result in the loss of functional dependency preservation, unlike 3NF which guarantees both lossless join and dependency preservation.

Deep Dive: ER to Relational Mapping U1 erDiagram EMPLOYEE ||--o{ DEPENDENT : "has (weak)" EMPLOYEE { string EmpID PK } DEPENDENT { string DepName PK "Partial" } Strong entities map directly to tables. Weak entities map to tables using a composite key: their own partial key + the strong entity's primary key. M:N relationships require a separate junction table. Example: The DEPENDENT table uses `(EmpID, DepName)` as its primary key. Pro-Tip: In total participation, foreign key constraints often use `ON DELETE CASCADE` to maintain consistency.

Normalization Applied Example Applied Concept Given: R(Student, Subject, Teacher, Mentor) with FDs: Student → Mentor, Mentor → Subject, Subject → Teacher. Check 3NF: Student → Mentor is fine (Student is a candidate key). But Mentor → Subject has a non-prime determinant (Mentor) that is not a superkey, violating 3NF. Decomposition into 3NF: R1(Mentor, Subject) — from Mentor → Subject R2(Subject, Teacher) — from Subject → Teacher R3(Student, Mentor) — from Student → Mentor (preserves candidate key)
Unit II: Relational Database Concepts CO2

Relational Algebra Core U2 A procedural query language defining execution steps. Core operators include Selection (σ, row filter), Projection (π, column filter), Cartesian Product (×), Set Difference (-), and Union (∪). Example: `π_name(σ_age>20(Student))` filters students older than 20, projecting only their names. Exam Trap: Union compatibility requires relations to have identical degree (number of attributes) and compatible domains.

Advanced Relational Algebra U2 Derived operators simplify queries: Natural Join (⋈) implicitly matches common attributes, and Division (÷) identifies universal quantification scenarios (e.g., "all"). Example: `Students ÷ Courses` returns students who have enrolled in EVERY available course. Pro-Tip: The Division operator is technically derived using Projection, Set Difference, and Cartesian Product.

Tuple vs Domain Relational Calculus U2 Calculus is non-procedural (describes WHAT to fetch, not HOW). TRC evaluates on a per-tuple basis. DRC evaluates attributes using domain variables. Example (TRC): `{t | t ∈ Student ∧ t.age > 20}`. Exam Trap: Unsafe queries (like infinite sets `{t | ¬(t ∈ Student)}`) are possible in calculus but syntactically disallowed in safe TRC systems.
Unit III: Structured Query Language (SQL) CO3

SQL Execution Pipeline U3 flowchart LR F[FROM] --> W[WHERE] --> G[GROUP BY] --> H[HAVING] --> S[SELECT] --> O[ORDER BY] Understanding logical execution order prevents semantic errors. `WHERE` filters rows prior to aggregation, while `HAVING` filters aggregated buckets. Example: You cannot use a column alias defined in `SELECT` inside the `WHERE` clause, because `WHERE` executes first. Pro-Tip: This is why `COUNT(*)` in `WHERE` throws an error; aggregation hasn't happened yet!

Correlated Subqueries U3 An inner query that references columns from the outer query. It executes row-by-row iteratively for each tuple processed by the outer query, degrading performance. Example: `SELECT * FROM Emp e1 WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Emp e2 WHERE e1.Dept = e2.Dept)` Exam Trap: Contrast with non-correlated subqueries which execute exactly once. Use `EXISTS` instead of `IN` for correlated lookups to short-circuit execution.

Triggers & Views U3 Views are virtual tables providing logical independence. Triggers execute procedural code in response to DML events (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), typically enforcing complex business rules. Example: `CREATE TRIGGER BeforeDelete BEFORE DELETE ON Users FOR EACH ROW ...` Pro-Tip: A "Mutating Table Error" occurs when a row-level trigger attempts to query the same table that invoked it.

DDL, DML, DCL & TCL Commands Applied Concept Category Purpose Example DDL (Data Definition) Define/modify schema CREATE TABLE Students (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50)); DML (Data Manipulation) Query/modify data INSERT INTO Students VALUES (1, 'Nihal'); DCL (Data Control) Manage permissions GRANT SELECT ON Students TO user1; TCL (Transaction Control) Manage transactions COMMIT; / ROLLBACK; / SAVEPOINT sp1;

Types of Joins Applied Concept Join Type Returns INNER JOIN Only rows with matching keys in both tables. LEFT OUTER JOIN All rows from left table + matched rows from right (NULLs for non-matches). RIGHT OUTER JOIN All rows from right table + matched rows from left. FULL OUTER JOIN All rows from both tables (NULLs where no match exists). CROSS JOIN Cartesian product of both tables (every row × every row). NATURAL JOIN Automatically joins on columns with the same name.
Unit IV: Transaction Processing CO4

ACID & Schedules U4 Transactions guarantee Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. Serializability ensures concurrent execution yields results identical to some serial sequence, preventing anomalies like Dirty Reads. Example: Using a Conflict Graph, if there's a cycle between transactions (e.g., T1 reads what T2 writes, and T2 reads what T1 writes), it is NOT conflict-serializable. Exam Trap: View serializability is less strict than conflict serializability and accommodates blind writes (writing without reading).

Deadlock Prevention (Wait-Die vs Wound-Wait) U4 stateDiagram-v2 state Wait-Die(Non-Preemptive) { OlderTxn --> YoungerTxn : Waits YoungerTxn --> OlderTxn : Dies (Rollback) } state Wound-Wait(Preemptive) { OlderTxn2 --> YoungerTxn2 : Wounds (Preempts) YoungerTxn2 --> OlderTxn2 : Waits } Using timestamps to prevent deadlocks: Wait-Die allows older transactions to wait for younger ones, while younger ones die. Wound-Wait preempts (wounds) the younger transaction holding the lock. Example: In Wound-Wait, if T1 (older) requests a lock held by T2 (younger), T2 is aborted and its locks are released to T1. Pro-Tip: A transaction that "dies" or is "wounded" retains its original timestamp upon restart, ensuring it eventually becomes the oldest and completes without starvation.

ARIES Crash Recovery U4 Utilizes Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) with Steal/No-Force buffer policies. The protocol executes three phases: Analysis, REDO (repeats history to reconstruct crash state), and UNDO (rolls back uncommitted txns). Example: Log Sequence Numbers (LSNs) link chain records. The REDO phase re-applies logs starting from the RedoLSN found in the checkpoint. Exam Trap: Compensation Log Records (CLRs) are written during the UNDO phase to ensure that if a crash occurs *during* recovery, UNDO operations are not repeated.
Unit V: Advanced DB & MongoDB CO5

CAP Theorem & NoSQL U5 Distributed systems can strictly guarantee only two out of Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance. NoSQL systems scale horizontally and typically relax Consistency (AP) or Availability (CP). Example: MongoDB operates as a CP system by default (elects a primary, halts writes if partition causes primary loss). Exam Trap: Network partitions (P) are unavoidable in distributed systems. Therefore, the real architectural choice is always between C and A.

MongoDB Documents & BSON U5 MongoDB eschews rigid relational schemas in favor of dynamic BSON (Binary JSON) documents. Data modeling shifts from normalization (joining tables) to embedding (storing related data inside a single document). Example: `{ _id: 1, name: "Alice", address: { city: "NY", zip: "10001" } }` Pro-Tip: Embed data for 1:1 or 1:few relationships to optimize read performance. Reference data for 1:Many or N:M to avoid hitting the 16MB document size limit.

Aggregation Pipeline U5 A multi-stage framework for data transformation, analogous to SQL `GROUP BY` and `JOIN`. Documents pass through stages like `$match` (filter), `$group` (aggregate), and `$project` (reshape). Example: `db.sales.aggregate([{ $match: { status: "A" } }, { $group: { _id: "$item", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } }])` Exam Trap: Stage order drastically impacts performance! Always place `$match` and `$sort` stages as early as possible to leverage indexes and reduce the dataset flowing into memory-intensive `$group` stages. ﻿

chunks: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a paradigm centered around "objects" (which contain data in the form of fields and code in the form of methods) rather than "actions" or logic. The six pillars (or core concepts) of OOP are: Class Object Encapsulation Abstraction Inheritance Polymorphism

title: Differentiate between a class and an object with one suitable example.
chunks: Class Object A logical template or blueprint. A physical entity/instance created from a class. Does not allocate memory when created. Allocates memory in the heap when instantiated. title: Define encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism.
chunks: Encapsulation: Wrapping data (variables) and code (methods) together into a single unit (class), protecting the data from outside interference. Abstraction: Hiding internal implementation details and exposing only the necessary functionalities to the user. Inheritance: A mechanism where a new class (child) inherits properties and behaviors from an existing class (parent), promoting code reusability. Polymorphism: The ability of a single entity (method, object, or operator) to take on multiple forms and behave differently based on the context.

title: What is the difference between procedural and object-oriented programming?
chunks: Procedural Programming (POP) Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) Program is divided into small parts called functions . Program is divided into parts called objects . Follows a Top-Down approach. Follows a Bottom-Up approach. Data is freely moving and less secure. Data is hidden (encapsulated) and highly secure. Example: C, Pascal Example: Java, C++, Python

title: What are JDK, JRE, and JVM?
chunks: JDK (Java Development Kit): A full software development environment. It contains the JRE plus development tools like the compiler ( javac ) and debugger. JRE (Java Runtime Environment): The environment required to run Java programs. It contains the JVM and core class libraries. JVM (Java Virtual Machine): An abstract machine that executes Java Bytecode. It makes Java platform-independent.

title: What is bytecode, and why is Java considered platform-independent?
chunks: Bytecode is a highly optimized set of instructions generated by the Java compiler ( javac ) after compiling the source code. It is not machine code, but rather intermediate code. Java is platform-independent because the compiler generates this bytecode instead of native machine code. This bytecode can be executed on any operating system as long as that system has a JVM (Java Virtual Machine) installed to interpret it (Write Once, Run Anywhere).

title: What is a Java package? Give two examples of commonly used packages.
chunks: A Java package is a mechanism for organizing related classes and interfaces into a single namespace. It prevents naming conflicts and controls access (encapsulation). Two Examples: java.util (Contains utility classes like Scanner, ArrayList) java.lang (Contains core classes like String, Math. It is imported automatically)
subject: java

title: List the four access modifiers in Java and state the default access level.
chunks: The four access modifiers in Java (from most restrictive to least) are: private (accessible only within the same class) default (no keyword; accessible only within the same package) protected (accessible within the same package and subclasses in other packages) public (accessible from anywhere) If no modifier is specified, the access level is default (package-private).
subject: java

title: What is a class and what is an object in Java? Give one difference between them.
chunks: A class is a user-defined blueprint or prototype from which objects are created. An object is a runtime instance of a class that has state and behavior. Difference: A class is a logical entity that consumes no memory upon declaration, whereas an object is a physical entity that consumes memory space in the heap when instantiated.

title: What is the purpose of the new keyword in Java? Where is the newly created object stored?
chunks: The new keyword in Java is used to create a new object or array by allocating memory at runtime. It essentially instantiates a class. Storage: The newly created object is always stored in the Heap memory.

title: What is the difference between an instance variable and a local variable? State any two differences.
chunks: Instance Variable Local Variable Declared inside a class but outside any method. Declared inside a method, constructor, or block. Gets a default value (e.g., 0 for int) if not initialized. Does not get a default value; must be initialized before use.

title: What is a constructor in Java? State any two rules of a constructor.
chunks: A constructor is a special block of code that is called automatically when an object is instantiated. It is used to initialize the state of the object. Rules: The constructor name must exactly match the class name. A constructor must not have an explicit return type (not even void ).

title: What is constructor overloading? On what basis does the compiler distinguish overloaded constructors?
chunks: Constructor Overloading is a technique of having more than one constructor in a class with different parameter lists. It allows objects to be initialized in different ways. The compiler distinguishes them based on the number of parameters , the types of the parameters , and the order of the parameters .

title: What is constructor chaining? Name the two keywords used for constructor chaining.
chunks: Constructor chaining is the process of calling one constructor from another constructor with respect to the current object. It helps avoid duplicate code. The two keywords used are: this() : Used to call a constructor of the same class. super() : Used to call a constructor of the superclass (parent class).

title: What is the purpose of the this keyword in Java? State any two uses.
chunks: The this keyword is a reference variable that refers to the current object on which the method or constructor is being invoked. Two Uses: To resolve shadowing when instance variables and local parameters share the same name (e.g., this.name = name; ). To invoke another constructor in the same class (using this() ).

title: What is Garbage Collection in Java? When does an object become eligible for garbage collection?
chunks: Garbage Collection (GC) is the process by which Java programs perform automatic memory management, freeing up the heap by deleting objects that are no longer in use. An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when it is completely unreferenced (i.e., no live thread can access it). This happens if its reference is set to null , if it is created anonymously, or if references are reassigned.
subject: java

title: What is autoboxing and unboxing in Java?
chunks: Autoboxing: The automatic conversion that the Java compiler makes between the primitive types and their corresponding object wrapper classes (e.g., converting int to Integer ). Unboxing: The reverse process; converting an object of a wrapper type back to its corresponding primitive value (e.g., converting Integer to int ).

title: What is String immutability? State one benefit of immutable Strings.
chunks: String immutability means that once a String object is created, its value or state cannot be changed. Any operation that alters the string creates a brand new String object rather than modifying the original. Benefit: It makes Strings thread-safe and allows caching in the String Constant Pool, which saves memory.

title: Define inheritance. List the different types of inheritance supported in Java.
chunks: Inheritance is a mechanism where a new class acquires the properties and methods of an existing class, establishing an IS-A relationship and promoting code reuse. title: What is the purpose of the super keyword? List any two uses.
chunks: The super keyword is a reference variable used to refer to the immediate parent class object. Two Uses: To invoke the immediate parent class constructor (e.g., super(); ). To invoke an overridden method in the parent class (e.g., super.display(); ).

title: Define method overloading and method overriding.
chunks: Method Overloading: Creating multiple methods in the same class with the same name but different parameters (compile-time polymorphism). Method Overriding: Providing a specific implementation in a subclass for a method that is already defined in its parent class. The method signature must be identical (run-time polymorphism).

title: What is polymorphism? Name its two types.
chunks: Polymorphism is the ability of an object or method to take on many forms, allowing the same interface to be used for different underlying forms (data types). Two Types: Compile-time Polymorphism (Static binding, e.g., Method Overloading). Run-time Polymorphism (Dynamic binding, e.g., Method Overriding).

title: What is dynamic binding? Why is it also called late binding?
chunks: Dynamic Binding is the process where the compiler does not resolve the method call at compile time, but rather the JVM determines the actual method implementation to execute at runtime based on the actual object type. It is called late binding because the binding of the method call to the method body is delayed until the program is actually executing.

title: Define upcasting and downcasting in Java.
chunks: Upcasting: Casting a subclass reference variable to a superclass reference. This is done automatically and implicitly by the compiler. Downcasting: Casting a superclass reference variable back to a subclass reference. This must be done explicitly by the programmer and requires checking to prevent ClassCastException .

title: What is the purpose of the instanceof operator?
chunks: The instanceof operator is a binary operator used to test whether a given object is an instance of a specific class, subclass, or interface. It returns true or false . It is primarily used to check object types before attempting a downcast , preventing runtime exceptions.

title: What is an abstract class? What is an interface?

Interface: A completely "abstract class" that acts as a contract. In modern Java, it primarily contains abstract methods and static constants, though it can now have default methods. A class implements an interface.

chunks: Generics enable types (classes and interfaces) to be parameters when defining classes, interfaces and methods. title: Explain the Top-Down and Bottom-Up approaches with a suitable example.
chunks: Top-Down Approach: The problem is broken down into smaller sub-problems. It focuses on the main algorithm first, then the details (used in Procedural Programming like C). Example: Building a car by first designing the full car, then breaking it down into engine, wheels, and doors. Bottom-Up Approach: The smaller modules or objects are designed first, and then integrated together to form the complete system (used in Object-Oriented Programming like Java). Example: Designing the engine, wheels, and doors first as independent objects, then assembling them to build the car.

title: Explain Java's platform independence in detail, from source code compilation to bytecode execution through the JVM.
chunks: Java's "Write Once, Run Anywhere" capability relies on its two-step execution process: Compilation: The developer writes Program.java (Source Code). The Java Compiler ( javac ) compiles this into Program.class . Instead of compiling it into machine-specific code (like C++), it compiles it into Bytecode . This bytecode is entirely independent of the underlying OS or hardware. Execution: The compiled bytecode is transported to any machine (Windows, Mac, Linux). That machine must have a JVM (Java Virtual Machine) installed. The JVM reads the bytecode and translates it into the specific machine-level instructions native to that exact operating system. Therefore, while the JVM is platform- dependent , the Java program (bytecode) itself is totally platform- independent .

Unit I: Introduction & Basics CO1

JVM Ecosystem & Internals Java compiles to bytecode, making it platform-independent (WORA). The ClassLoader Subsystem handles dynamic class loading, linking, and initialization. The Execution Engine parses bytecode using an Interpreter and a JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler. javac App.java // Produces App.class (Bytecode) java App // JVM Execution Engine runs Bytecode Trap: ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError. ClassNotFoundException is thrown during explicit dynamic loading (e.g., Class.forName() ). NoClassDefFoundError occurs if a class was present at compile-time but is missing at runtime during implicit loading.

Data Types & Memory Semantics Primitives reside on the Thread Stack; Objects reside on the Shared Heap. Java explicitly defines sizes regardless of the OS (e.g., int is always 32-bit). Object references themselves are passed by value (a copy of the reference is passed). int x = 5; // Stack primitive Integer y = Integer.valueOf(5); // Heap object reference on stack Pro Tip: Autoboxing & Constant Pool. Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; a == b is TRUE because integers between -128 and 127 are cached in the IntegerCache. Outside this range, they are distinct objects!

JVM Architecture Diagram flowchart TD A[Java Source Code] --> B[Javac Compiler] B --> C[Bytecode .class] C --> D[ClassLoader Subsystem] D --> E[Runtime Data Areas: Heap, Stack, Metaspace] E --> F[Execution Engine: Interpreter + JIT]

Explain the Top-Down and Bottom-Up approaches with a suitable example. Applied Concept Top-Down Approach: The problem is broken down into smaller sub-problems. It focuses on the main algorithm first, then the details (used in Procedural Programming like C). Example: Building a car by first designing the full car, then breaking it down into engine, wheels, and doors. Bottom-Up Approach: The smaller modules or objects are designed first, and then integrated together to form the complete system (used in Object-Oriented Programming like Java). Example: Designing the engine, wheels, and doors first as independent objects, then assembling them to build the car.
Unit II: Core Mechanics & OOP CO2

Polymorphism & Dynamic Dispatch Method overloading is compile-time polymorphism (Static Binding). Method overriding is runtime polymorphism (Dynamic Dispatch/Binding), utilizing the vtable to invoke the subclass implementation. super is used to invoke the overridden superclass method. Parent obj = new Child(); obj.display(); // Calls Child's display() at runtime Trap: Method Hiding. You cannot override static methods. If a child class defines the same static method, it hides the parent's method. The call is resolved at compile-time based on the reference type , not the object type!

Interfaces vs Abstract Classes Interfaces define contracts (can have default and static methods since Java 8). Abstract classes can hold state (instance variables) and constructors. A class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one class. interface Flyer { default void land() { /* body */ } } abstract class Bird { abstract void sing(); } Pro Tip: The Diamond Problem. If a class implements two interfaces with identical default methods, the compiler forces you to override the method and explicitly invoke the desired interface's method using InterfaceName.super.method() .

Constructors & Initialization Blocks Instance Initialization Blocks (IIB) run before the constructor but after the call to super() . Static blocks run once when the class is loaded by the ClassLoader. Constructors can be chained using this() . class Demo { static { System.out.println("Static Init"); } { System.out.println("Instance Init"); } Demo() { System.out.println("Constructor"); } }

Define Object-Oriented Programming and list the six pillars of OOP. Applied Concept Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a paradigm centered around "objects" (which contain data in the form of fields and code in the form of methods) rather than "actions" or logic. The six pillars (or core concepts) of OOP are: Class Object Encapsulation Abstraction Inheritance Polymorphism

Differentiate between a class and an object with one suitable example. Applied Concept Class Object A logical template or blueprint. A physical entity/instance created from a class. Does not allocate memory when created. Allocates memory in the heap when instantiated. Declared using the class keyword. Created using the new keyword. Example: If Car is a class (the blueprint), then a Red Tesla Model S is an object (an actual car).

List the four access modifiers in Java and state the default access level. Applied Concept The four access modifiers in Java (from most restrictive to least) are: private (accessible only within the same class) default (no keyword; accessible only within the same package) protected (accessible within the same package and subclasses in other packages) public (accessible from anywhere) If no modifier is specified, the access level is default (package-private).

What is the purpose of the this keyword in Java? State any two uses. Applied Concept The this keyword is a reference variable that refers to the current object on which the method or constructor is being invoked. Two Uses: To resolve shadowing when instance variables and local parameters share the same name (e.g., this.name = name; ). To invoke another constructor in the same class (using this() ).
Unit III: Memory, Multithreading & Concurrency CO3

Garbage Collection & Memory Tuning GC reclaims unreachable objects. The Heap is divided into Young Gen (Eden, S0, S1) and Old Gen. Objects surviving multiple Minor GCs are promoted. ZGC and G1GC are modern concurrent collectors minimizing pause times. System.gc(); // Suggests GC, doesn't guarantee it. // TLABs (Thread-Local Allocation Buffers) speed up Eden allocation. Trap: Memory Leaks. Java can have memory leaks if strong references to unused objects are maintained (e.g., an ever-growing static HashMap ). The GC will not clear them!

Thread Synchronization & Visibility synchronized utilizes intrinsic locks (monitors) to guarantee mutual exclusion. The volatile keyword guarantees memory visibility across threads by reading/writing directly to Main Memory instead of CPU caches, but it does NOT guarantee atomicity. volatile boolean flag = true; synchronized(this) { count++; } // Prevents Race Conditions Pro Tip: Happens-Before Relationship. A write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that field. This prevents instruction reordering by the JIT compiler and CPU, ensuring safe publication.

Thread Lifecycle Diagram stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> NEW NEW --> RUNNABLE : start() RUNNABLE --> RUNNING : Thread Scheduler RUNNING --> WAITING : wait(), join() WAITING --> RUNNABLE : notify() RUNNING --> BLOCKED : sync block BLOCKED --> RUNNABLE : Lock acquired RUNNING --> TERMINATED : run() completes

What is the purpose of the super keyword? List any two uses. Applied Concept The super keyword is a reference variable used to refer to the immediate parent class object. Two Uses: To invoke the immediate parent class constructor (e.g., super(); ). To invoke an overridden method in the parent class (e.g., super.display(); ).

Explain built-in and user-defined packages with suitable examples. Also explain the purpose of the import statement. Applied Concept Built-in Packages: Provided by the Java API. Example: java.util , java.io . User-defined Packages: Created by the programmer to group related classes. Example: package com.mycompany.utils; Import Statement: Used to bring a class or an entire package into visibility so it can be used without typing its fully qualified name (e.g., import java.util.Scanner; ).
Unit IV: Collections Framework & Generics CO4

Generics & Type Erasure Generics provide compile-time type safety. Type Erasure means the JVM removes generic type info during compilation to maintain backward compatibility, replacing them with upper bounds or Object . You cannot instantiate a generic array ( new T[] ). List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); // Compiles to: List list = new ArrayList(); Trap: Covariance vs Contravariance (PECS). List<Object> is NOT a supertype of List<String> . Use wildcards: ? extends T for Producer (read-only), ? super T for Consumer (write-only).

Collections Internals (HashMap) HashMap computes the hash of the key to find the bucket array index. If collisions occur, it forms a LinkedList. To prevent DoS attacks via collision degradation, Java 8 introduced the Treeification Threshold (8) , transforming lists into Red-Black Trees for O(log n) lookup. Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>(); map.put("Key", 1); // Uses hashCode() and equals() Pro Tip: ConcurrentHashMap. Instead of locking the entire map (like HashTable ), ConcurrentHashMap uses CAS (Compare-And-Swap) operations and synchronizes only the specific node (bucket) being updated, allowing high concurrency.
Collections Hierarchy Diagram flowchart TD Iterable --> Collection Collection --> List Collection --> Set Collection --> Queue List --> ArrayList List --> LinkedList Set --> HashSet Map --> HashMap
Unit V: Exceptions & Modern Java 8+ Features CO5

Exception Handling & Hierarchy Throwable is the root. Error (JVM crash) and RuntimeException (logic bugs) are Unchecked . Everything else (e.g., IOException ) is Checked and must be handled. try-with-resources automatically closes objects implementing AutoCloseable . try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("x.txt"))) { br.readLine(); } catch (IOException e) { /* handled */ } Trap: Finally Overwrite. If a try block returns a value (e.g., 5), but the finally block also has a return statement (e.g., 10), the finally block silently overwrites the result. The method returns 10!

Lambdas & Streams API Streams enable declarative data processing. Intermediate operations ( filter , map ) are lazy and do nothing until a Terminal operation ( collect , reduce ) is invoked. Lambdas ( -> ) implement Functional Interfaces (SAM: Single Abstract Method). List<Integer> evens = list.stream() .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0) // Lazy Intermediate .collect(Collectors.toList()); // Terminal Execution Pro Tip: invokedynamic. Lambdas are NOT anonymous inner classes. The compiler uses the invokedynamic bytecode instruction to generate the lambda implementation dynamically at runtime, heavily optimizing memory and class-loading overhead.

String Pool & Immutability String objects are immutable; modifying one creates a new instance. String literals are stored in the String Constant Pool to save memory. Using partial fractions: (2 - x) / ((1 - x)(1 - 2x)) = A / (1 - x) + B / (1 - 2x) . Solving gives A = -1 and B = 3 . Thus, G(x) = -1/(1 - x) + 3/(1 - 2x) . Solution: a n = 3(2 n ) - 1 .
subject: maths

title: Solve the following recurrence relation: a_{n+2} - 7a_{n+1} + 12a_n = 0, given a_1 = 2, a_2 = 7.
chunks: Characteristic equation: r^2 - 7r + 12 = 0 ⇒ (r - 3)(r - 4) = 0 . Roots: 3, 4. General solution: a n = c 1 3 n + c 2 4 n . Using conditions: 3c 1 + 4c 2 = 2 and 9c 1 + 16c 2 = 7 . Multiply first by 4: 12c 1 + 16c 2 = 8 . Subtracting the second gives 3c 1 = 1 ⇒ c 1 = 1/3 . Then 4c 2 = 2 - 1 = 1 ⇒ c 2 = 1/4 . Solution: a n = 3 n-1 + 4 n-1 .
subject: maths

title: Solve the following recurrence relation: a_n - 5a_{n-1} + 7a_{n-2} - 3a_{n-3} = 0; a_0 = 2, a_1 = 5, a_2 = 12
chunks: Characteristic equation: r^3 - 5r^2 + 7r - 3 = 0 . Roots: 1, 1, 3 . General solution: a n = c 1 + c 2 n + c 3 3 n . Solving conditions: c 1 + c 3 = 2 , c 1 + c 2 + 3c 3 = 5 , c 1 + 2c 2 + 9c 3 = 12 . We get c 1 = 1, c 2 = 1, c 3 = 1 . Solution: a n = 1 + n + 3 n .

title: Solve the following recurrence relation: a_{n+3} - 5a_{n+2} + 8a_{n+1} - 4a_n = 0, given a_1 = 2, a_2 = 5, a_3 = 14
chunks: Characteristic equation: r^3 - 5r^2 + 8r - 4 = 0 . Roots: 1, 2, 2 . General solution: a n = c 1 + (c 2 + c 3 n)2 n . Solving with conditions gives c 1 = 5, c 2 = -3, c 3 = 1.5 . Solution: a n = 5 + (-3 + 1.5n)2 n .

title: Solve the following recurrence relation by using generating function: a_n = 2a_{n-1} + 3a_{n-2} given a_0 = 1, a_1 = 2
chunks: Let G(x) be the generating function. G(x) - 1 - 2x = 2x(G(x) - 1) + 3x^2 G(x) . G(x)(1 - 2x - 3x^2) = 1 ⇒ G(x) = 1 / ((1 - 3x)(1 + x)) . Using partial fractions: 1 / ((1 - 3x)(1 + x)) = A / (1 - 3x) + B / (1 + x) gives A = 3/4 , B = 1/4 . Solution: a n = (3/4)3 n + (1/4)(-1) n .

title: Solve the following recurrence relation: a_{n+3} - 5a_{n+2} + 8a_{n+1} - 4a_n = 0 given a_1 = 1, a_2 = 4, a_3 = 11

title: Solve the following recurrence relation by using generating function: a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2} given a_0 = 0, a_1 = 1

Unit I: Propositional Logic CO1

Fundamental Logic Operators Connectives establish truth-functional relationships between propositions. Master implications (\(p \rightarrow q\)) and biconditionals (\(p \leftrightarrow q\)), as they form the bedrock of mathematical proofs. Example: "If it rains (p), then the ground is wet (q)." \(p \rightarrow q\).

Logical Equivalences De Morgan's Laws (\(
eg(p \land q) \equiv 
eg p \lor 
eg q\)) and Implication Equivalence (\(p ightarrow q \equiv 
eg p \lor q\)) are pivotal for simplifying compound propositions without brute-force truth tables. Example: "It's false that I am cold AND tired" equals "I am not cold OR I am not tired."

Predicates & Quantifiers Examiner Trick: Nested Quantifiers. Remember that \(\forall x \exists y\) is NOT equivalent to \(\exists y \forall x\). The order dictates dependency! Universal (\(\forall\)) implies all elements in the domain; Existential (\(\exists\)) asserts at least one exists. Negating them flips the quantifier. Example: \(\neg(\forall x P(x)) \equiv \exists x \neg P(x)\).

Rules of Inference Modus Ponens (\(p, p \rightarrow q \vdash q\)) and Modus Tollens (\(\neg q, p \rightarrow q \vdash \neg p\)) validate arguments syntactically. Niche Topic: Fallacy of Affirming the Consequent. Given \(p \rightarrow q\) and \(q\), concluding \(p\) is invalid. Example: If it rains, ground is wet. Ground is wet. Therefore, it rained (Invalid!).

Symbolic Translations (Propositional Logic) Applied Concept Understanding how to convert English to symbolic logic and vice-versa. Example: "It is not raining but I wear a raincoat" translates to \(\neg p \land r\). (Note: 'but' translates to logical AND). Example: \((p \lor q) \land \neg r\): "It is raining or I carry an umbrella, and I do not wear a raincoat."

Specific Truth Tables Applied Concept Recognizing Tautologies directly from truth tables. Example: \((p \rightarrow q) \lor (q \rightarrow p)\) evaluates to True in all cases (Tautology). Example: \((p \rightarrow q) \leftrightarrow (\neg q \rightarrow \neg p)\) is also a Tautology, illustrating the contrapositive equivalence.

Conditional Statements Truth Values Applied Concept A conditional statement (\(p \rightarrow q\)) is false only when \(p\) is True and \(q\) is False. Example: "If 1 + 1 = 3, then 2 + 2 = 5" is True (False \(\rightarrow\) False). Example: "If 1 + 1 = 2, then dogs can fly" is False (True \(\rightarrow\) False).

Permutations & Equations Applied Concept Applying factorial definitions to solve for unknowns. Example: Solving \((n + 1)P_3 = 5 \times nP_2\). Expanding gives \(\frac{(n+1)!}{(n-2)!} = 5 \times \frac{n!}{(n-2)!}\). Canceling \((n-2)!\) and \(n!\) leaves \(n + 1 = 5 \implies n = 4\).
Unit II: Counting Methods CO2

Pigeonhole Principle If \(N\) items are placed into \(k\) boxes, at least one box contains \(\lceil N/k \rceil\) items. Crucial for existence proofs without direct construction. Example: Among 13 people, at least 2 were born in the same month.

Combinatorics: Stars and Bars Niche Topic: Stars & Bars (Multiset Coefficients). Finds non-negative integer solutions to \(x_1 + x_2 + ... + x_k = n\). Formula is \(C(n + k - 1, k - 1)\). Applies when items are indistinguishable but bins are distinct. Example: Distributing 10 identical candies among 3 children: \(C(10+3-1, 3-1) = 66\).

Linear Recurrence Relations Characterize sequences via previous terms. Solve \(a_n = c_1a_{n-1} + c_2a_{n-2}\) using the characteristic equation \(r^2 - c_1r - c_2 = 0\). Example: Fibonacci \(a_n = a_{n-1} + a_{n-2}\) gives roots \((1 \pm \sqrt{5})/2\).

Generating Functions Examiner Trick: Using partial fraction decomposition to extract coefficients from \(G(x) = \sum a_n x^n\). Translates sequence convolution into polynomial multiplication, elegantly solving non-homogeneous recurrences. Example: Sequence 1, 1, 1... corresponds to \(1/(1-x)\).

Solving Generating Functions Applied Concept Mapping generating functions back to sequences. Example: The generating function \(G(x) = \frac{1}{1 - 2x}\) takes the form \(\frac{1}{1 - rx}\), which corresponds to the sequence \(a_n = r^n\). Here, \(r = 2\), so the solution is \(a_n = 2^n\).

Applied Recurrence Relations Applied Concept Solving specific forms and initial value problems. Example: \(a_n = 10a_{n-1} - 25a_{n-2}\). Characteristic equation: \(r^2 - 10r + 25 = 0 \implies (r - 5)^2 = 0\). Root is \(r = 5\) (repeated). Form: \(a_n = (c_1 + c_2n)5^n\). Example: Non-linear relation \(a_n = a_{n-1}^2\). If \(a_1 = 2\), then \(a_2 = 4, a_3 = 16\).
Unit III: Graph Theory CO3

Handshaking Lemma The sum of degrees of all vertices equals \(2|E|\). A foundational invariant proving odd-degree vertices must occur in pairs. Example: A graph with 5 vertices of degree 3 cannot exist since \(15 \neq 2|E|\).

Euler & Hamilton Paths Examiner Trick: Euler traverses all edges exactly once; Hamilton traverses all vertices exactly once. Do not conflate them! Euler circuits require all vertices to have an even degree. Hamiltonian has no simple definitive check (NP-complete). Example: \(K_3\) has both paths, but \(K_{2,3}\) is not Hamiltonian. graph TD A((Odd)) --- B((Odd)) A --- C((Even)) B --- C C --- D((Even)) C --- E((Even)) D --- E

Graph Isomorphism Two graphs are isomorphic if a bijection preserves adjacency. Invariants: vertex count, edge count, and degree sequence. Example: A square and a 4-cycle drawn as a figure-eight are isomorphic.

Bipartite Graphs & Matching Niche Topic: Hall's Marriage Theorem. A bipartite graph \(G=(V_1, V_2, E)\) has a complete matching for \(V_1\) iff \(|N(S)| \ge |S|\) for all \(S \subseteq V_1\). A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd-length cycles. Example: Assigning 3 workers to 3 tasks optimally without overlap.
Unit IV: Set Theory & Relations CO4

Set Operations & Power Sets Operations include union, intersection, difference, and symmetric difference (\(\oplus\)). The power set \(\mathcal{P}(S)\) contains all subsets. Example: If \(S = \{1, 2\}\), \(\mathcal{P}(S) = \{\emptyset, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 2\}\}\). Size is \(2^n\).

Equivalence Relations A relation must be reflexive (\(xRx\)), symmetric (\(xRy \implies yRx\)), and transitive (\(xRy \land yRz \implies xRz\)). Forms equivalence classes. Example: Congruence modulo \(n\), where \(a \equiv b \pmod n\) divides \(\mathbb{Z}\) into \(n\) classes.

Partial Orderings (Posets) Examiner Trick: Hasse Diagrams. Ensure you remove reflexive loops and transitive edges to depict minimal/maximal elements accurately. Requires reflexivity, antisymmetry (\(xRy \land yRx \implies x=y\)), and transitivity. Example: The "divides" relation on integers forms a poset, visualizable via Hasse. graph BT 1 --> 2 1 --> 3 2 --> 6 3 --> 6

Injective, Surjective, Bijective Niche Topic: Cardinality mappings. If a bijection exists between two sets, they share the same cardinality (\(\aleph_0\) for countably infinite). Injective (1-to-1): no two \(x\) map to same \(y\). Surjective (onto): every \(y\) is mapped. Bijective: both, thus invertible. Example: \(f(x) = 2x\) from \(\mathbb{R}\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) is bijective.
Unit V: Trees & Automata CO5
Tree Properties A tree is a connected, undirected graph with no simple circuits. It inherently possesses \(n-1\) edges for \(n\) vertices. Example: A hierarchical file system directory structure.

Spanning Trees Examiner Trick: Kruskal's vs Prim's. Both find Minimum Spanning Trees, but Kruskal sorts edges globally while Prim expands locally from a node. A subgraph that contains all vertices and is a tree. Critical for optimizing network routing with minimal cost. Example: Connecting 5 cities with the least amount of copper wire.

Finite State Machines (FSMs) Niche Topic: Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages. Used exclusively to prove a language is NOT regular by demonstrating string repetition violations. DFAs have exactly one transition per state-symbol pair. NFAs allow multiple. They are computationally equivalent in expressive power. Example: A vending machine dispensing a soda only after exactly 50 cents is inserted. stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> q0 q0 --> q1: 1 q1 --> q0: 0 q1 --> q2: 1 q2 --> [*]
Boolean Algebra A distributive lattice representing logical operations. Simplification uses consensus theorem and Karnaugh maps to minimize circuit gates. Example: \(AB + AB' = A(B + B') = A\). ﻿
